stufe_0_frage: What is new on my desk?
stufe_1_frage: Is that always true – and how exact is it?
stufe_3_frage: How does alternating voltage become a steady direct voltage?
stufe_4_frage: How does a quiet signal become loud?
stufe_5_frage: What can an amplifier with two inputs do?
stufe_6_frage: One chip for clock and time?
stufe_8_frage: How does a light barrier work?
lex_zdiode: A Zener diode conducts in the forward direction like any diode. Connected the other way round it only blocks up to its Zener voltage (4.7 V or 5.6 V, printed on it) – above that it conducts and holds the voltage almost fixed. It always needs a series resistor.
lex_transistor_pnp: A PNP transistor works like the NPN transistor, only with reversed signs: the emitter is at plus, and it conducts when a small current flows out of the base. Same board with B, C and E twice; the case is marked »P«.
lex_spule: A coil is a wound-up wire. It resists every change of current: when switched on the current rises slowly, when switched off it wants to keep flowing. There is one with 100 mH and one with an iron core with 1 H (henry).
lex_trimmer: A trimmer is a small potentiometer for adjusting: the wiper s divides the track between a and b. It is set once with a screwdriver – tap it and the slider appears.
lex_ir_led: An IR LED glows in the infrared – our eyes cannot see this light. Like every LED it needs a series resistor. The camera of many phones shows its glow.
lex_fototransistor: A phototransistor is a transistor controlled by light: the more light or IR radiation falls on it, the more current it lets through from C to E. You can shade it with the cover card.
lex_optokoppler: An optocoupler contains an IR LED and a phototransistor in a dark case. When the LED glows (A and K), the transistor conducts (C and E) – without the two circuits being connected.
lex_spannungsregler: A voltage regulator turns a higher, fluctuating DC voltage into exactly 5 V. The input (IN) needs at least about 1.7 V more than the output (OUT). On a short circuit or overheating it protects itself and delivers less current.
lex_opmodul: The op-amp module (operational amplifier) compares its inputs IN+ and IN−. If IN+ is higher, the output goes up, otherwise down. With resistors from the output back to IN− it becomes an amplifier with an exactly adjustable gain. Limits in the model: the output stays about 1.5 V below plus and above minus. It changes by at most 0.5 V per microsecond and delivers at most about 25 mA. At 1 MHz it only amplifies once. Below 4 V supply it does not work.
lex_timer555: The 555 timer is a chip with eight legs. It compares the voltage on a capacitor with one third and two thirds of the supply and switches its output accordingly. With two resistors and a capacitor it becomes a clock, with one a short-time alarm. In the model it works from 4.5 V. Its output reaches up to about 1.7 V below plus and down to about 0.1 V. If R is below about 0.7 V, the output is always off.
lex_blinkmodul: The blink module switches its output on and off again and again. Inside there is a multivibrator made of two transistors and two 22 µF electrolytic capacitors. In »Inside the blink module« you build it yourself.
lex_tonmodul: The tone module plays a little melody as long as its input gets current. It is a behaviour model: Volta does not calculate every part inside it. »Inside the tone module« shows how a tone comes out of a multivibrator.
lex_zeitmodul: After a short press on »start« the timer module switches its output on for a few seconds. In Volta 2 the 555 timer takes over this job. There you set the time yourself with R and C.
lex_verstaerkermodul: The amplifier module turns a tiny current at the input into a large one at the output. Inside there are two transistors one after the other. It switches well, but does not amplify music cleanly. That is what the op-amp module is for.
lex_messstelle_v: The voltage measuring point V shows the voltage between its two legs right at the part. Connect it in parallel, next to the part whose voltage you want to know. It hardly loads the circuit (10 MΩ).
lex_messstelle_a: The current measuring point A shows the current flowing through it. Connect it in series: the current has to pass through it. In parallel with a battery it would be a short circuit.
lex_messstelle_ohm: The resistance measuring point Ω sends a small test current through the part between its legs and shows the resistance. Only measure without any other voltage, so with the circuit switched off.
lex_tastkopf: The probe K1 or K2 connects a field to the oscilloscope. It has only one leg: it always measures against 0V. Like a real probe, it hardly loads the circuit (10 MΩ). The peak value and frequency are shown at the probe.
exp2_0_1_titel: Measuring without a tangle of cables
exp2_0_1_frage: A small lamp is glowing. How much voltage is across it, and how much current flows through it? Can you measure both at the same time?
exp2_0_1_v1: No, you can only measure one thing at a time.
exp2_0_1_v2: Yes, with two measuring points both work at once.
exp2_0_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_0_1_b1: Both measuring points showed something at the same time: volts and milliamperes.
exp2_0_1_b2: Only one measurement worked at a time.
exp2_0_1_b3: I'm not sure what the displays showed.
exp2_0_1_s1: Plug the current measuring point A into A1 and A2. Plug the lamp into A2 and A3.
exp2_0_1_s2: Draw a red wire from V+ to A1 and a black one from A3 to 0V. Switch on the main switch.
exp2_0_1_s3: Plug the voltage measuring point V into B2 and B3. Connect B2 to A2 and B3 to A3. The twin meter shows both values and the power.
exp2_0_1_h1: The current measuring point belongs in the circuit. The current has to flow through it.
exp2_0_1_h2: The voltage measuring point belongs next to the lamp: one leg on each side.
exp2_0_1_loesung: V+ to A1, current measuring point on A1 and A2, lamp on A2 and A3, A3 to 0V. Voltage measuring point on B2 and B3, plus wires from A2 to B2 and from A3 to B3.
exp2_0_1_erklaerung: You measure voltage next to the part and current in the circuit. With two measuring points you see both at once. Voltage times current gives the power. It tells you how much energy the lamp gets every second. It is measured in watts (W), here in milliwatts (mW).
exp2_0_1_mehr: With a real meter you have to move the plugs when you switch from voltage to current. The measuring points stay fixed in the circuit. The voltage measuring point takes almost no current. The current measuring point has almost no resistance. So neither of them disturbs the circuit much.
exp2_0_1_w1: Set the battery to 3 V. How do voltage, current and power change?
exp2_0_1_w2: Work out the power yourself: voltage times current. Do you get the same as the display?
exp2_0_1_echt: With two simple meters you can measure voltage and current at the same time on a flat battery and a small lamp for real. Ask an adult to help you set them up.
exp2_0_2_frage: Only very little current flows through a large resistor. Which measuring range shows it most precisely?
exp2_0_2_v1: The largest range, everything fits in there.
exp2_0_2_v2: The smallest range that the value still fits into.
exp2_0_2_v3: It doesn't matter, the display is always equally precise.
exp2_0_2_b1: In the smallest range that fitted, the display had the most digits.
exp2_0_2_b2: The display was most precise in the largest range.
exp2_0_2_s1: Plug the current measuring point A into A1 and A2 and the 10 kΩ resistor into A2 and A4. Connect V+ to A1 and A4 to 0V. Switch on the main switch.
exp2_0_2_s2: Tap the range on the current display. Choose 200 mA, then 20 mA, then 2 mA. How many digits do you see?
exp2_0_2_s3: Plug the voltage measuring point V into B2 and B4. Connect B2 to A2 and B4 to A4. Choose the 2 V range on the voltage display. What does it show now?
exp2_0_2_h1: A small range shows more digits after the decimal point.
exp2_0_2_h2: If there is only a »1« at the front, the value is too big for the range. Then choose the next larger one.
exp2_0_2_loesung: For the current, 2 mA fits best: about 0.450 mA. For the voltage, 20 V fits: about 4.5 V. In the 2 V range the display only shows »1«.
exp2_0_2_erklaerung: Every measuring range has an upper limit. If the value is below it, the display shows it. In the smallest range that fits, it has the most digits and is most precise. If the value is too big, there is only a »1« at the front. This is called overflow: you need the next larger range.
exp2_0_2_mehr: If the range is set to »automatic«, the meter chooses it by itself. Real meters need a moment for this. If you choose the range yourself, you know exactly how many digits you get. That matters when measuring.
exp2_0_2_w1: Set it back to »automatic«. Which range does the display choose?
exp2_0_2_w2: Take a 1 kΩ resistor. Which current range fits best now?
exp2_0_2_echt: Many simple meters have a rotary switch for the range. Try out with an adult on a flat battery what the overflow looks like.
exp2_0_3_frage: Two batteries are connected one after the other. You connect the middle between them to 0V. What voltage does the end at the second battery show?
exp2_0_3_v1: Also a positive voltage, just a smaller one.
exp2_0_3_v3: 0 V, because the middle is at 0V.
exp2_0_3_b1: The end of the second battery showed a negative voltage.
exp2_0_3_b2: It showed a positive voltage there.
exp2_0_3_s1: The desk now has battery 2 with the terminals +B2 and −B2. Connect both +B2 and 0V to field C5. That is the middle.
exp2_0_3_s2: Plug the lamp into A1 and A2. Draw a red wire from V+ to A1 and a blue one from −B2 to A2. Switch on the main switch.
exp2_0_3_s3: Show the voltage at A1, C5 and A2. What does A2 show?
exp2_0_3_h1: The voltage display measures every field against 0V.
exp2_0_3_h2: The end at −B2 is 4.5 V below the middle.
exp2_0_3_loesung: V+ to A1, lamp on A1 and A2, −B2 to A2, +B2 and 0V to C5. Then A1 shows about +4.5 V, C5 shows 0 V and A2 about −4.5 V.
exp2_0_3_erklaerung: A voltage is always measured between two points. The display compares every field with 0V. If 0V is in the middle, one side is 4.5 V higher and the other 4.5 V lower: −4.5 V. Together there are 9 V across the lamp.
exp2_0_3_mehr: Many amplifiers need plus and minus with a middle in between. Then their output can swing above and below the middle, just like a sound. You will need this later with the operational amplifier.
exp2_0_3_w1: Set battery 2 to 9 V. What does A2 show now? How bright is the lamp?
exp2_0_3_w2: Remove the wire from 0V to C5. What happens to the lamp and the voltages?
exp2_0_3_echt: With an adult you can connect two flat batteries one after the other. A meter with its black lead on the middle shows plus at one end and minus at the other.
exp2_1_1_frage: At one field the current splits between two resistors. How are the current before it and the two currents after it related?
exp2_1_1_v1: The two currents after it add up to the current before it.
exp2_1_1_v2: Each current after it is as big as the current before it.
exp2_1_1_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_1_1_b1: The two currents together were exactly as big as the current before.
exp2_1_1_b2: Each branch had the whole current.
exp2_1_1_s1: Plug a current measuring point into A1 and A3. Connect V+ to A1. At field A3 the current will split.
exp2_1_1_s2: Plug a second current measuring point into A3 and B3. After it comes the 1 kΩ resistor on B3 and B5. Connect B5 to 0V.
exp2_1_1_s3: Plug a third current measuring point into A3 and A5. After it comes the 2.2 kΩ resistor on A5 and A7. Connect A7 to 0V and switch on the main switch.
exp2_1_1_h1: Every current measuring point has to sit in the path of the current, not next to it.
exp2_1_1_h2: Show all three currents one after the other on the twin meter and add up the last two.
exp2_1_1_loesung: Before the junction about 13.1 mA flow. About 9.0 mA flow through 1 kΩ and about 4.1 mA through 2.2 kΩ. Together that is 13.1 mA again.
exp2_1_1_erklaerung: At a junction no current gets lost and none is added. What flows in flows out again. This is the junction rule. The larger part flows through the smaller resistor.
exp2_1_1_mehr: Gustav Robert Kirchhoff wrote this rule down in 1845. It is also called Kirchhoff's first law. It holds at every point of every circuit, even inside a computer chip.
exp2_1_1_w1: Swap the 2.2 kΩ resistor for a 1 kΩ one. How does the current split now?
exp2_1_1_w2: Add a third branch at A3. Does the rule still hold?
exp2_1_1_echt: With one meter you can measure the currents one after the other for real. To do so you have to open the circuit each time. Ask an adult to help you.
exp2_1_2_frage: Three resistors are connected one after the other to 9 V. Each one gets part of the voltage. What do the three parts add up to?
exp2_1_2_v1: Together they add up to exactly the battery voltage.
exp2_1_2_v2: Together they are more than 9 V.
exp2_1_2_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_1_2_b1: The three voltages together were as big as the battery voltage.
exp2_1_2_b2: Together they were more than 9 V.
exp2_1_2_s1: Plug the resistors in: 1 kΩ on A1 and A3, 2.2 kΩ on A3 and A5 and 4.7 kΩ on A5 and A7. Connect V+ to A1 and A7 to 0V.
exp2_1_2_s2: Connect A1 to B1, A3 to B3, A5 to B5 and A7 to B7. Plug three voltage measuring points into B1 and B3, B3 and B5, and B5 and B7.
exp2_1_2_s3: Switch on the main switch. Show the three voltages and add them up.
exp2_1_2_h1: Each voltage measuring point sits next to exactly one resistor.
exp2_1_2_h2: The largest voltage is across the largest resistor.
exp2_1_2_loesung: About 1.14 V are across 1 kΩ, about 2.51 V across 2.2 kΩ and about 5.35 V across 4.7 kΩ. Together that is 9.00 V.
exp2_1_2_erklaerung: If you go once around the loop, the battery voltage is shared among all the parts. Together the partial voltages add up to exactly the battery voltage. This is the loop rule. The larger resistor gets the larger voltage.
exp2_1_2_mehr: This rule also comes from Kirchhoff. It is called Kirchhoff's second law. Resistors in a row are also called a voltage divider. With it you can get 3 V out of 9 V, for example.
exp2_1_2_w1: Also measure the voltage of the battery itself: plug a voltage measuring point between A1 and A7.
exp2_1_2_w2: Swap two resistors. How do the voltages change?
exp2_1_2_echt: Three resistors, a flat battery and a meter are enough to check the rule for real. Ask an adult to help you.
exp2_1_3_frage: The curve tracer slowly turns the voltage up and down again and records the current. What line does it draw for a resistor?
exp2_1_3_v1: A curve that gets steeper and steeper.
exp2_1_3_v2: A straight line through the middle.
exp2_1_3_v3: I don't know – I'll let it draw.
exp2_1_3_b1: It drew a straight line through the middle.
exp2_1_3_b2: The line got steeper and steeper.
exp2_1_3_b3: I couldn't make sense of the line.
exp2_1_3_s1: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and A2. Connect KS+ to A1. Then connect A2 to KS−.
exp2_1_3_s2: Tap »Plot« on the curve tracer. Voltage goes to the right, current goes up.
exp2_1_3_s3: Tap »Keep«. Then swap the resistor for a 470 Ω one. How does the line change?
exp2_1_3_h1: The curve tracer has its own power supply. It doesn't need the battery.
exp2_1_3_h2: Double the voltage, double the current: that makes a straight line.
exp2_1_3_loesung: KS+ to A1, resistor on A1 and A2, A2 to KS−. With 1 kΩ exactly 6.7 mA flow at 6.7 V. The line is straight.
exp2_1_3_erklaerung: With a resistor the current grows just like the voltage. Double the voltage means double the current. That is why the curve tracer draws a straight line. The smaller the resistor, the steeper it is. This is Ohm's law: I = U / R.
exp2_1_3_mehr: There is a series resistor inside the curve tracer. It protects the part. That is why the voltage at the part doesn't quite reach the set value. At 10 V and 20 mA it is 500 Ω, so about 6.7 V reach the 1 kΩ resistor.
exp2_1_3_w1: Set it to one direction only. What is missing from the picture now?
exp2_1_3_w2: Try a 10 kΩ resistor. How flat does the line get?
exp2_1_3_echt: Real curve tracers are found in labs and workshops. At home you can measure a characteristic curve point by point: with a control knob, a meter and an adult.
exp2_1_4_titel: Why the lamp has no straight line
exp2_1_4_frage: A small lamp is connected to the curve tracer. Does it draw a straight line again, as with the resistor?
exp2_1_4_v1: Yes, a lamp is just a resistor too.
exp2_1_4_v2: No, the line gets flatter towards the outside.
exp2_1_4_v3: I don't know – I'll let it draw.
exp2_1_4_b1: The line was steep in the middle and got flatter towards the outside.
exp2_1_4_b2: It was a straight line like the resistor's.
exp2_1_4_b3: I couldn't make sense of the line.
exp2_1_4_s1: Plug the lamp into A1 and A2. Connect KS+ to A1. Then connect A2 to KS−.
exp2_1_4_s2: Set the curve tracer to 10 V and 50 mA. Tap »Plot«.
exp2_1_4_s3: Tap »Keep«. Then swap the lamp for a 220 Ω resistor. Compare the two lines.
exp2_1_4_h1: The wire in the lamp gets hot when a lot of current flows.
exp2_1_4_h2: Hot wire has a larger resistance. Then the current grows more slowly.
exp2_1_4_loesung: KS+ to A1, lamp on A1 and A2, A2 to KS−. At low voltage the line is steep, at high voltage it gets flatter. The hotter the lamp is, the more it holds back the current.
exp2_1_4_erklaerung: The thin wire in the lamp gets hot when a lot of current flows. Hot metal has a larger resistance than cold metal. That is why the current doesn't grow as fast as the voltage. The line bends to the side. So a lamp is not a fixed resistor.
exp2_1_4_mehr: When it is cold, a lamp has a much smaller resistance than when it is hot. So for a moment a much larger current flows when you switch it on. That is why light bulbs usually burn out exactly when they are switched on.
exp2_1_4_w1: Change from 50 mA to 20 mA. The lamp gets less hot. What does the line look like now?
exp2_1_4_w2: Watch the lamp while it is drawing. When does it glow brightly, when is it dark?
exp2_1_4_echt: Measure a lamp from a craft shop while it is cold, with a meter set to »Ω«. The value is much smaller than when it is lit. Ask an adult to help you.
exp2_1_5_frage: An LED is connected to the curve tracer. It drives the current first one way, then the other. Does the LED conduct in both directions?
exp2_1_5_v1: No, only in one direction, and only above a certain voltage.
exp2_1_5_v3: I don't know – I'll let it draw.
exp2_1_5_b1: The current flowed in one direction only, and only above a certain voltage.
exp2_1_5_b2: The current flowed in both directions.
exp2_1_5_b3: I couldn't make sense of the line.
exp2_1_5_s1: Plug the red LED into A1 and A2, with the long leg on A1. Connect KS+ to A1. Then connect A2 to KS−.
exp2_1_5_s2: Set the curve tracer to 5 V and 20 mA. Tap »Plot«. At what voltage does current start to flow?
exp2_1_5_s3: Tap »Keep«. Then swap the red LED for another colour or for a diode. Where does the line bend now?
exp2_1_5_h1: Left of the middle is the reverse direction. The line stays flat there.
exp2_1_5_h2: The point where the line bends upwards is called the threshold voltage.
exp2_1_5_loesung: KS+ to A1, LED with the long leg on A1, A2 to KS−. The red LED conducts from about 1.9 V, the blue one only from about 3 V. The diode already conducts from about 0.7 V. No current flows backwards.
exp2_1_5_erklaerung: A diode is a valve for current. In the reverse direction it lets almost nothing through. In the forward direction it only conducts above the threshold voltage, but then very well. Every LED colour has its own threshold voltage. Blue needs the most.
exp2_1_5_mehr: The colour of an LED depends on the material it is made of. Blue light has more energy than red light and therefore needs more voltage. A real LED can only take a few volts backwards. That is why the curve tracer is set to 5 V here.
exp2_1_5_w1: Set it to one direction only. Now the line shows only the forward direction.
exp2_1_5_w2: Plug the LED in the wrong way round. What happens to the line?
exp2_1_5_echt: With a flat battery, a 470 Ω resistor and LEDs of different colours you can see it for real: the LED only lights up the right way round. Ask an adult to help you.
exp2_1_6_frage: A battery has 9 V. Does it stay at 9 V when two lamps draw current from it?
exp2_1_6_v1: No, the voltage drops a little.
exp2_1_6_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_1_6_b1: With the lamps the voltage was a little lower than without.
exp2_1_6_b2: The voltage stayed exactly the same.
exp2_1_6_s1: Plug a voltage measuring point into A1 and B1. Connect V+ to A1 and B1 to 0V. Switch on the main switch. What does the display show?
exp2_1_6_s2: Plug two lamps into A3 and A4 and into B3 and B4. Connect A3 to B3, A4 to B4 and B4 to 0V.
exp2_1_6_s3: Connect A1 to S1 and S2 to A3. Switch the switch S on and off. How does the voltage change?
exp2_1_6_h1: Choose the 20 V range on the display. Then you see two digits after the decimal point.
exp2_1_6_h2: Watch the last digit when you flip the switch.
exp2_1_6_loesung: Without a load the battery shows 9.00 V. With both lamps it is only about 8.86 V.
exp2_1_6_erklaerung: Every battery has a small resistance inside it, the internal resistance. When current flows, part of the voltage is lost across it. Then a little less is left at the terminals. The more current flows, the more the voltage drops.
exp2_1_6_mehr: In Volta each cell has 0.25 Ω, so the 9 V battery has 1.5 Ω. At about 90 mA, about 0.14 V are lost across it. An old battery has a larger internal resistance. Without a load it often still shows almost the full voltage, but under load it gives way a lot.
exp2_1_6_w1: Take one lamp away. Does the voltage drop less now?
exp2_1_6_w2: Work out the internal resistance: lost voltage divided by current. A current measuring point will help you.
exp2_1_6_echt: Measure a flat battery for real, once without and once with a small lamp. With an old battery the difference is especially big. Ask an adult to help you.
exp2_2_1_frage: The oscilloscope draws the voltage as a curve over time. What does the battery look like on it? And the blinker?
exp2_2_1_v2: The battery is a straight line. The blinker jumps up and down.
exp2_2_1_v3: I don't know – I'll take a look.
exp2_2_1_b1: I saw a wavy line for both.
exp2_2_1_b2: K1 showed a straight line. K2 jumped back and forth between two levels.
exp2_2_1_b3: I couldn't see anything on the screen.
exp2_2_1_s1: Plug the 470 Ω resistor into A3 and A4. Plug the red LED from A4 to B4 (long leg on A4).
exp2_2_1_s2: Connect V+ to the plus of the blinker module (M1) and 0V to the minus (M2). Connect V+ to A3. Then connect B4 to the output of the module (M3).
exp2_2_1_s3: Plug probe K1 onto A3 and probe K2 onto B4. Switch on the main switch and look at the oscilloscope.
exp2_2_1_h1: Each probe measures against 0V. You only need to put its tip on a field.
exp2_2_1_h2: One square to the right takes half a second. So the whole screen shows 5 seconds.
exp2_2_1_loesung: K1 on A3 shows a straight line at almost 9 V. K2 on B4 jumps back and forth: almost 0 V when the LED is lit, and about 7.7 V when it is off. Such an angular curve is called a square wave.
exp2_2_1_erklaerung: A meter only shows a number. The oscilloscope shows how the voltage changes over time. Voltage goes up, time goes to the right. A battery does not change, so its line is straight. The blinker switches on and off, so its curve jumps.
exp2_2_1_mehr: The word oscilloscope means something like »looking at oscillations«. In the past, an electron beam drew the curve on a glass tube. Today a computer chip works out the curve.
exp2_2_1_w1: Press a shorter time base on the oscilloscope. What does the square wave look like then?
exp2_2_1_w2: Put K2 on A4 instead of B4. What changes in the curve?
exp2_2_1_echt: A real oscilloscope is expensive. Maybe a school or a hobby club has one. Ask there if you may look at a blinker once.
exp2_2_2_frage: The generator makes an alternating voltage at 100 Hz. How long does one oscillation take then?
exp2_2_2_v1: One hundredth of a second, so 10 ms.
exp2_2_2_v3: I don't know – I'll read it off.
exp2_2_2_s1: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and A3. Connect G to A1. Then connect A3 to G0.
exp2_2_2_s2: Plug probe K1 onto A1. The generator is set to sine with 100 Hz and 2 V peak.
exp2_2_2_s3: One square on the screen takes 2 ms. Count the squares from one hill to the next hill.
exp2_2_2_h1: The generator does not need the main switch. G0 is fixed to 0V.
exp2_2_2_h2: Work it out: squares times 2 ms gives the time of one oscillation.
exp2_2_2_loesung: From hill to hill there are 5 squares of 2 ms, so 10 ms. 100 oscillations of 10 ms make exactly one second. The peak is about 1.9 V instead of 2 V, because the generator has 50 Ω inside.
exp2_2_2_erklaerung: The time for one oscillation is called the period. The number of oscillations in one second is called the frequency. It is measured in hertz (Hz). The shorter the period, the higher the frequency: frequency = 1 divided by the period.
exp2_2_2_mehr: The unit hertz is named after Heinrich Hertz. In 1886 he was the first to produce and detect radio waves. The mains current in Europe oscillates at 50 Hz.
exp2_2_2_w1: Set the generator to triangle and then to square. Does the period stay the same?
exp2_2_2_w2: Set 200 Hz. How many squares does one oscillation take now?
exp2_2_2_echt: A swing oscillates too. Use a clock to time how long one swing there and back takes. Then you know its period.
exp2_2_3_frage: The generator plays a tone through the loudspeaker. What happens to the tone when you raise the frequency?
exp2_2_3_b1: With a higher frequency the tone got higher.
exp2_2_3_b3: I couldn't hear or see a difference.
exp2_2_3_s1: Connect G to A1. Connect A1 to LS1.
exp2_2_3_s2: Connect LS2 to A2. Then connect A2 to G0. Plug probe K1 onto A1.
exp2_2_3_s3: Set the generator to sine with 440 Hz and 2 V peak. Listen and look at the loudspeaker and the oscilloscope. Then turn the frequency higher and lower.
exp2_2_3_h1: Is your sound off? The loudspeaker still shows the pitch as a number in Hz.
exp2_2_3_h2: The current has to flow through the loudspeaker: from G via LS1 and LS2 back to G0.
exp2_2_3_loesung: At 440 Hz you hear the note A. The loudspeaker shows 440 Hz. One oscillation takes about 2.3 ms. On A1 the peak is only about 0.28 V: the loudspeaker has 8 Ω, the generator 50 Ω inside.
exp2_2_3_erklaerung: The cone of the loudspeaker moves exactly in time with the voltage. It pushes the air back and forth, and you hear that as a tone. More oscillations per second give a higher tone. So the pitch is the frequency.
exp2_2_3_mehr: Musicians often tune their instruments to the note A at 440 Hz. Young people hear from about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. As people get older, they hear high tones less well.
exp2_2_3_w1: Set 880 Hz. That is twice the value. Does the tone sound like the A, only higher?
exp2_2_3_w2: Set the generator to square. How does the tone sound now?
exp2_2_3_echt: Some apps play tones at a frequency you can set. Try out which tones you can still hear. Always keep the volume low.
exp2_2_4_frage: The oscilloscope shows a peak of 4 V. What does the meter show for the same alternating voltage?
exp2_2_4_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_2_4_b2: The meter showed less than the peak, about 2.8 V.
exp2_2_4_s1: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and A3. Connect G to A1. Then connect A3 to G0.
exp2_2_4_s2: Plug the voltage measuring point V into B1 and B3. Connect A1 to B1 and A3 to B3. Plug probe K1 onto A1.
exp2_2_4_s3: Set the generator to sine with 50 Hz and 4 V peak. Tap ⎓ on the meter until it shows ~. Compare the number with the peak on the oscilloscope.
exp2_2_4_h1: With ⎓ the meter shows the average. For an alternating voltage it is almost 0 V.
exp2_2_4_h2: With ~ the meter shows the RMS value. Divide the peak by 1.41 and compare.
exp2_2_4_loesung: The oscilloscope shows a peak of about 3.98 V. The meter on ~ shows about 2.81 V. That is the peak divided by 1.41.
exp2_2_4_erklaerung: An alternating voltage is at its peak only for a very short time. So the meter shows the RMS value. It says: this alternating voltage warms a resistor as much as a direct voltage of the same size. For a sine, the RMS value is the peak divided by 1.41.
exp2_2_4_mehr: The number 1.41 is the square root of 2. The mains socket has 230 V RMS. Its peak is about 325 V. That is why the socket is so dangerous: never touch it!
exp2_2_4_w1: Set the generator to square. How big is the RMS value now compared with the peak?
exp2_2_4_w2: Set the meter back to ⎓. What does it show, and why?
exp2_2_4_echt: Many power supplies say which alternating voltage they need from the socket. Read it together with an adult. Never open a power supply or a socket.
exp2_2_5_frage: A capacitor is connected to the generator. What happens to the current when the frequency rises?
exp2_2_5_v1: At a higher frequency more current flows.
exp2_2_5_v2: At a higher frequency less current flows.
exp2_2_5_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_2_5_b1: With a higher frequency more current flowed.
exp2_2_5_b2: With a higher frequency less current flowed.
exp2_2_5_b3: The current always stayed the same.
exp2_2_5_s1: Plug the current measuring point into A1 and A3. Plug the 1 µF capacitor into A3 and A5.
exp2_2_5_s2: Connect G to A1. Then connect A5 to G0. Tap ⎓ on the meter until it shows ~.
exp2_2_5_s3: Set the generator to sine and 4 V peak. Read the current at 100 Hz. Then set 1000 Hz and read it again.
exp2_2_5_h1: The current measuring point belongs in the path of the current, in front of the capacitor.
exp2_2_5_h2: With ⎓ you see almost 0 mA, because the current keeps changing direction.
exp2_2_5_loesung: At 100 Hz about 1.8 mA flow. At 1000 Hz about 16.6 mA flow. Ten times the frequency, almost ten times the current.
exp2_2_5_erklaerung: Direct current does not get through a capacitor. With alternating voltage, though, it is charged and discharged all the time. The faster this happens, the more current flows back and forth. So at a high frequency the capacitor lets a lot of current through.
exp2_2_5_mehr: The resistance of a capacitor to alternating current is called reactance. It is 1 divided by (2 · π · f · C). With 1 µF and 1000 Hz that is about 160 Ω.
exp2_2_5_w1: Take a 100 nF capacitor. How much current flows now at 1000 Hz?
exp2_2_5_w2: Set 5000 Hz. Does the current keep rising?
exp2_2_5_echt: In many loudspeaker boxes there is a capacitor in front of the small tweeter. It only lets the high tones through. Maybe you can see it in a broken box that an adult opens for you.
exp2_2_6_frage: Now a coil is connected to the generator. What happens to the current here when the frequency rises?
exp2_2_6_v1: Like the capacitor: more frequency, more current.
exp2_2_6_v2: Exactly the other way round: more frequency, less current.
exp2_2_6_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_2_6_b1: With a higher frequency more current flowed.
exp2_2_6_b2: With a higher frequency less current flowed.
exp2_2_6_b3: The current always stayed the same.
exp2_2_6_s1: Plug the current measuring point into A1 and A3. Plug the 100 mH coil into A3 and A5.
exp2_2_6_s2: Connect G to A1. Then connect A5 to G0. Tap ⎓ on the meter until it shows ~.
exp2_2_6_s3: Set the generator to sine and 4 V peak. Read the current at 1000 Hz. Then set 100 Hz and read it again.
exp2_2_6_h1: The current measuring point belongs in the path of the current, in front of the coil.
exp2_2_6_h2: Compare with the capacitor from the last experiment.
exp2_2_6_loesung: At 1000 Hz only about 4.4 mA flow. At 100 Hz about 27 mA flow. With the coil it is exactly the other way round from the capacitor.
exp2_2_6_erklaerung: A coil resists every change in the current. The faster the current has to change direction, the more strongly it brakes. So at a high frequency the coil lets little current through. It lets direct current through almost unbraked.
exp2_2_6_mehr: The coil also has a reactance. It is 2 · π · f · L. With 100 mH and 1000 Hz that is about 630 Ω. On top of that comes the resistance of the wire, here 30 Ω.
exp2_2_6_w1: Take the 1 H coil. How much current flows now at 100 Hz?
exp2_2_6_w2: Set 10 Hz. Does the current get even bigger?
exp2_2_6_echt: In loudspeaker boxes there is often a coil in front of the big woofer. It only lets the low tones through. Together with the capacitor it splits up the tones.
exp2_2_7_frage: A resistor and a capacitor form an RC circuit. Which frequencies arrive weaker at the output A3?
exp2_2_7_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_2_7_b1: At high frequencies the curve on A3 was smaller.
exp2_2_7_b2: At low frequencies the curve on A3 was smaller.
exp2_2_7_b3: The curve on A3 was always the same size.
exp2_2_7_s1: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and A3. Plug the 100 nF capacitor into A3 and A5.
exp2_2_7_s2: Connect G to A1. Then connect A5 to G0. Plug probe K1 onto A1 and K2 onto A3.
exp2_2_7_s3: Set the generator to sine and 4 V peak. Compare K1 and K2 at 100 Hz and at 3200 Hz. At the end, set 1600 Hz.
exp2_2_7_h1: K1 shows what goes in. K2 shows what arrives at the output.
exp2_2_7_h2: Next to each channel is the peak-to-peak value. Compare the two numbers.
exp2_2_7_loesung: At 100 Hz almost everything arrives at A3. At 1600 Hz there are still about 5.3 V peak-to-peak instead of 7.8 V, so about two thirds. At 3200 Hz there are only about 3.2 V.
exp2_2_7_erklaerung: At a high frequency the capacitor lets a lot of current through to G0. Then little voltage is left at A3. Low frequencies get through almost unweakened. That is why the circuit is called a low-pass filter.
exp2_2_7_mehr: The cut-off frequency is fc = 1 divided by (2 · π · R · C). With 1 kΩ and 100 nF that is about 1600 Hz. There, about 70 percent of the voltage still arrives. A low-pass filter makes music sound dull.
exp2_2_7_w1: Take a 470 nF capacitor. Where is the cut-off frequency now?
exp2_2_7_w2: Connect the loudspeaker to the output. Does a square wave sound softer after the low-pass filter?
exp2_2_7_echt: A radio or a music system often has a treble control. Turn it all the way down. The music then sounds dull, as if through a wall.
exp2_2_8_frage: Now you swap the resistor and the capacitor. Which frequencies arrive weaker at the output A3 now?
exp2_2_8_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_2_8_b1: At low frequencies the curve on A3 was smaller.
exp2_2_8_b2: At high frequencies the curve on A3 was smaller.
exp2_2_8_b3: The curve on A3 was always the same size.
exp2_2_8_s1: Plug the 100 nF capacitor into A1 and A3. Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A3 and A5.
exp2_2_8_s2: Connect G to A1. Then connect A5 to G0. Plug probe K1 onto A1 and K2 onto A3.
exp2_2_8_s3: Set the generator to sine and 4 V peak. Compare K1 and K2 at 100 Hz and at 3200 Hz. At the end, set 1600 Hz.
exp2_2_8_h1: The capacitor is now in front, the resistor behind it to G0.
exp2_2_8_h2: Next to each channel is the peak-to-peak value. Compare the two numbers.
exp2_2_8_loesung: At 100 Hz only about 0.5 V peak-to-peak arrives at A3. At 1600 Hz there are about 5.3 V, as with the low-pass filter. At 3200 Hz there are already about 6.4 V.
exp2_2_8_erklaerung: At a low frequency the capacitor lets hardly any current through. Then there is hardly any voltage across the resistor, and little arrives at A3. High frequencies get through well. That is why the circuit is called a high-pass filter.
exp2_2_8_mehr: The cut-off frequency is the same as for the low-pass filter: about 1600 Hz. A high-pass filter takes away the bass. That way the small tweeter of a loudspeaker box only gets the high tones.
exp2_2_8_w1: Take a 10 kΩ resistor. Do the low tones get through better now?
exp2_2_8_w2: Build a low-pass and a high-pass filter one after the other. Which frequencies are left?
exp2_2_8_echt: Listen to music once through a small phone speaker and once through a big box. The small speaker plays hardly any bass. It works almost like a high-pass filter.
exp2_3_1_frage: Two LEDs are connected against each other to the AC source. One points to the right, the other to the left. Which one lights up?
exp2_3_1_v1: Only one – the one that is the right way round.
exp2_3_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_3_1_b2: Both lit up. In slow motion they took turns.
exp2_3_1_s1: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and A3. Plug the red LED from A3 to A5 (long leg on A3).
exp2_3_1_s2: Plug the green LED from B5 to B3 (long leg on B5). Connect A3 to B3 and A5 to B5.
exp2_3_1_s3: Connect W~a to A1 and B5 to W~b. Connect A5 to 0V and plug probe K1 onto A1. Switch on the main switch.
exp2_3_1_h1: The AC source needs the main switch. It is set to 6 V~.
exp2_3_1_h2: Set slow motion to 1/100. Then you can see what the two LEDs do.
exp2_3_1_loesung: Both LEDs light up, but taking turns. In each half of the oscillation up to 6.7 mA flow through one of them. On the oscilloscope you see a sine on A1 from about −8.5 V to +8.5 V.
exp2_3_1_erklaerung: At the AC source, plus and minus keep swapping, 50 times every second. Sometimes W~a is plus, sometimes W~b. Each LED lets the current through in one direction only. So first one lights up, then the other. That is too fast for our eyes, so we see both lit.
exp2_3_1_mehr: 6 V~ is the RMS value. The peak is 1.41 times as big, so about 8.5 V. The AC source has no fixed pole at 0V. Only the wire from A5 to 0V gives the oscilloscope a reference.
exp2_3_1_w1: Remove the wire from A5 to 0V. What does the oscilloscope show now?
exp2_3_1_w2: Set the AC source to 9 V~. Do the LEDs get brighter?
exp2_3_1_echt: A bicycle dynamo on the front wheel also makes alternating voltage. When you ride slowly, the light flickers. In LED lamps a small circuit smooths the light.
exp2_3_2_frage: A diode sits between the AC source and a resistor. What arrives at the resistor?
exp2_3_2_v1: Only half: the arches pointing up.
exp2_3_2_v2: The whole wave, just a bit smaller.
exp2_3_2_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_3_2_b1: Only the arches pointing up arrived at the resistor.
exp2_3_2_b2: The whole wave arrived at the resistor.
exp2_3_2_b3: Nothing at all arrived at the resistor.
exp2_3_2_s1: Plug the diode from A1 to A3 (ring towards A3). Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A3 and A5.
exp2_3_2_s2: Connect W~a to A1. Connect A5 to W~b. Then connect A5 to 0V.
exp2_3_2_s3: Plug probe K1 onto A1 and K2 onto A3. Switch on the main switch and compare the two curves.
exp2_3_2_h1: The ring on the diode shows where the current may flow.
exp2_3_2_h2: K1 shows the alternating voltage before the diode, K2 the voltage after it.
exp2_3_2_loesung: K1 shows the whole wave from −8.5 V to +8.5 V. K2 shows only the arches pointing up, up to about 7.8 V. In between the voltage stays at 0 V. On average there are about 2.4 V across the resistor.
exp2_3_2_erklaerung: The diode lets the current through in one direction only. When W~a is plus, current flows through the resistor. When W~a is minus, the diode blocks. This turns the alternating voltage into a direct voltage that always points one way. But it has big gaps. This is called a half-wave rectifier.
exp2_3_2_mehr: The arches are about 0.7 V smaller than the wave before. That is how much voltage a silicon diode needs to conduct.
exp2_3_2_w1: Turn the diode round. What does K2 show now?
exp2_3_2_w2: Plug a voltage measuring point next to the resistor. What does the meter show with ⎓ and what with ~?
exp2_3_2_echt: Old chargers often had just one single diode. That was cheap, but the device hummed and got warm.
exp2_3_3_frage: Now you put four diodes together in a square. What arrives at the resistor now?
exp2_3_3_v1: Both halves. All arches point up.
exp2_3_3_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_3_3_b1: All arches pointed up, without gaps.
exp2_3_3_b3: Nothing at all arrived at the resistor.
exp2_3_3_s1: Plug in four diodes: from A1 to A3 and from A3 to A5, from C1 to C3 and from C3 to C5. On all of them the ring points to the right.
exp2_3_3_s2: Connect W~a to A3 and W~b to C3. Connect C5 to A5. Connect A1 to 0V and C1 to 0V.
exp2_3_3_s3: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A5 and A7. Connect A7 to 0V. Plug probe K1 onto A5 and switch on the main switch.
exp2_3_3_h1: The AC source is connected only to A3 and C3. It must not be connected to 0V.
exp2_3_3_h2: Plus comes out at A5, minus is 0V. Check that all the rings point to the right.
exp2_3_3_loesung: On A5 there are now arches up to about 7.1 V, all pointing up, without gaps. On average it is about 4.2 V, almost twice as much as with one diode. The arches come 100 times every second.
exp2_3_3_erklaerung: When W~a is plus, the current flows through the diode A3–A5 to the resistor and back through C1–C3. When W~b is plus, it takes the path through C3–C5 and A1–A3. Through the resistor the current always flows in the same direction. So the second half is used as well. This is a bridge rectifier.
exp2_3_3_mehr: The current always goes through two diodes. That is why the arches are about 1.4 V smaller than the peak of the alternating voltage. The bridge rectifier also comes ready-made as one part with four legs.
exp2_3_3_w1: Also connect W~b to 0V. Look at the diodes and the oscilloscope. Why must the AC source not be connected to 0V here?
exp2_3_3_w2: Take out one of the four diodes. What does the oscilloscope show now?
exp2_3_3_echt: Almost every power supply has a bridge rectifier. In an old, broken power supply you may find four diodes in a square. Only open it with an adult and never while it is plugged into the socket.
exp2_3_4_frage: An electrolytic capacitor goes after the bridge rectifier. What does it do to the arches?
exp2_3_4_v1: It fills up the valleys. The voltage becomes almost smooth.
exp2_3_4_v2: Nothing, the arches stay as they are.
exp2_3_4_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_3_4_b1: The voltage became almost smooth, only a small wobble was left.
exp2_3_4_b2: The arches stayed exactly the same.
exp2_3_4_s1: Build the bridge rectifier as in the last experiment. Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A5 and A7 and connect A7 to 0V.
exp2_3_4_s2: Plug the electrolytic capacitor into B5 and B7. Plus goes to B5. Connect A5 to B5 and B7 to A7.
exp2_3_4_s3: Plug probe K1 onto A5 and switch on the main switch. How big is the wobble now?
exp2_3_4_h1: On the electrolytic capacitor, the side with the minus stripe is minus. It goes to 0V.
exp2_3_4_h2: Next to the channel is the peak-to-peak value. That is the height of the wobble.
exp2_3_4_loesung: The voltage on A5 is now almost steady at about 6.6 V. It only wobbles by about 0.5 V. Without the capacitor it jumped back and forth between 0 V and 7.1 V.
exp2_3_4_erklaerung: At every peak the capacitor charges up quickly. In the valleys it gives its charge to the resistor. So the voltage only drops a little until the next peak comes. The wobble that is left is called ripple voltage.
exp2_3_4_mehr: The more current the load needs, the faster the capacitor discharges. With 470 Ω the voltage wobbles by about 1 V, with 220 Ω already by about 1.6 V. A bigger capacitor holds the voltage better.
exp2_3_4_w1: Take a 470 Ω or 220 Ω resistor. How big does the wobble get?
exp2_3_4_w2: Take a 10 kΩ resistor. How smooth is the voltage now?
exp2_3_4_echt: Sometimes you can hear a bad power supply hum, for example quietly in a loudspeaker. That is the ripple voltage at 100 Hz.
exp2_3_5_frage: A Zener diode is plugged in the wrong way round after a resistor on 9 V. What voltage is across it?
exp2_3_5_v1: Almost 9 V, because the wrong way round it blocks.
exp2_3_5_v2: About 4.7 V. Then it lets the current through.
exp2_3_5_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_3_5_b1: There were almost 9 V across the Zener diode.
exp2_3_5_b2: There were just under 5 V across the Zener diode.
exp2_3_5_b3: There was no voltage at all across the Zener diode.
exp2_3_5_s1: Plug the 470 Ω resistor into A1 and A3. Connect V+ to A1.
exp2_3_5_s2: Plug the 4.7 V Zener diode from A5 to A3 (ring towards A3). Connect A5 to 0V.
exp2_3_5_s3: Plug the voltage measuring point V into B3 and B5. Connect A3 to B3 and A5 to B5. Switch on the main switch.
exp2_3_5_h1: The ring of the Zener diode points to plus. That way it is in the reverse direction.
exp2_3_5_h2: Without the resistor too much current would flow. It must always be in front.
exp2_3_5_loesung: There are about 4.9 V across the Zener diode. About 8.8 mA flow through it. With 4.5 V on the battery it is about 4.1 V, with 3 V almost the whole 3 V.
exp2_3_5_erklaerung: In the reverse direction a Zener diode only blocks up to its Zener voltage. Above that it lets current through. The resistor takes the rest of the voltage. So the voltage across the Zener diode stays almost fixed, even if the battery has more.
exp2_3_5_mehr: The Zener diode is named after the physicist Clarence Zener. If the voltage is smaller than the Zener voltage, it blocks almost completely. Then it holds nothing fixed.
exp2_3_5_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V and then to 3 V. Does the Zener diode still hold the voltage?
exp2_3_5_w2: Take the 5.6 V Zener diode. What voltage do you measure now?
exp2_3_5_echt: Zener diodes are in many devices where a fixed voltage is needed. They look like normal diodes. The Zener voltage is printed on them in small letters.
exp2_3_6_frage: A voltage regulator is meant to always deliver 5 V. Does that work on 9 V and also on 4.5 V?
exp2_3_6_v1: Yes, it makes 5 V out of any voltage.
exp2_3_6_v2: Only if there is clearly more than 5 V at the input.
exp2_3_6_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_3_6_b1: With both batteries 5 V came out.
exp2_3_6_b2: With 9 V, 5 V came out, with 4.5 V less.
exp2_3_6_s1: Plug the voltage regulator into A3, A4 and A5 (IN on A3, OUT on A5). Connect V+ to A3 and A4 to 0V.
exp2_3_6_s2: Plug the 470 Ω resistor into A5 and A7. Connect A7 to 0V.
exp2_3_6_s3: Plug the voltage measuring point V into B5 and B7. Connect A5 to B5 and A7 to B7. Switch on and measure at 9 V and at 4.5 V. At the end, set 9 V again.
exp2_3_6_h1: The middle connection GND goes to 0V.
exp2_3_6_h2: You change the battery on the desk with the arrows.
exp2_3_6_loesung: At 9 V the regulator delivers exactly 5.0 V. About 10.6 mA flow through the resistor. At 4.5 V only about 3.0 V come out.
exp2_3_6_erklaerung: The regulator keeps comparing its output with 5 V. If the voltage is too high, it lets less current through. For that it needs about 1.7 V more at the input than at the output. When a 9 V battery runs down, the output stays at 5 V until it drops below about 6.7 V.
exp2_3_6_mehr: The extra voltage turns into heat in the regulator. It also takes about 3 mA for itself. Many microcontrollers need exactly 5 V or 3.3 V. That is why there is a voltage regulator almost everywhere.
exp2_3_6_w1: Take a 220 Ω resistor. Does the output stay at 5 V?
exp2_3_6_w2: Plug a current measuring point in front of IN and one after OUT. How much current does the regulator need for itself?
exp2_3_6_echt: A USB charger delivers 5 V. Inside, a circuit regulates the voltage in a very similar way, only more cleverly and with less heat.
exp2_3_7_frage: You build a power supply from the AC source, rectifier, capacitor and regulator. Do steady 5 V come out at the end?
exp2_3_7_v1: Yes, with 9 V~ steady 5 V come out.
exp2_3_7_v2: No, the wobble gets through to the output.
exp2_3_7_v3: I don't know – I'll build it.
exp2_3_7_b1: There were steady 5 V at the output.
exp2_3_7_b2: The voltage at the output wobbled.
exp2_3_7_s1: Build the bridge rectifier as in the experiment »Both halves«, but without the resistor. Plug the electrolytic capacitor into B5 and B6 (plus on B5). Connect A5 to B5.
exp2_3_7_s2: Plug the voltage regulator into C5, C6 and C7 (IN on C5). Connect B6 to C6 and C6 to 0V. Plug the 470 Ω resistor into C7 and C9 and connect C9 to 0V.
exp2_3_7_s3: Connect C7 to D7. Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into D7 and D9 and the green LED from D9 to D10 (long leg on D9). Connect D10 to C9. Plug K1 onto A5 and K2 onto C7 and switch on.
exp2_3_7_h1: The AC source is set to 9 V~. With 6 V~ the voltage is not enough.
exp2_3_7_h2: K1 shows the voltage on the capacitor, K2 the voltage at the output.
exp2_3_7_loesung: On the capacitor the voltage swings between about 9.5 V and 10.9 V. At the output there are steady 5.0 V. The green LED shows with about 3 mA that the power supply is running.
exp2_3_7_erklaerung: Each part has a job. The rectifier turns alternating voltage into arches in one direction. The capacitor fills up the valleys. The regulator cuts off the remaining wobble, because it always has enough voltage at its input.
exp2_3_7_mehr: Work it out: with 6 V~ the peak is about 8.5 V. Two diodes take away 1.4 V, the wobble another 1 V. Then in the valleys the regulator lacks the 1.7 V it needs. The output then drops to about 4.1 V.
exp2_3_7_w1: Set the AC source to 6 V~. What does K2 show now?
exp2_3_7_w2: Use a 220 Ω resistor at the output. How much does the voltage on the capacitor wobble now?
exp2_3_7_echt: With an adult, look at the rating plate of a plug-in power supply. It shows the input and the output. Never open it: there are 230 V in the socket.
exp2_4_1_titel: A small current controls a big current
exp2_4_1_frage: A small current flows into the base of the transistor. How big is the current it lets through at the collector?
exp2_4_1_v1: About as big as the base current.
exp2_4_1_v2: Much bigger, many hundred times as big.
exp2_4_1_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_4_1_b1: Both currents were about the same size.
exp2_4_1_b2: The collector current was about 200 times as big.
exp2_4_1_s1: Put the transistor on B3 (B top left, C top right, E at the bottom). Connect C3 to 0V.
