exp2_5_5_erklaerung: The op-amp keeps IN− at the same voltage as IN+. The resistors divide the output: only part of it reaches IN−. That is why the output has to be bigger. You calculate: gain = 1 + 47 kΩ : 10 kΩ = 5.7.
exp2_5_5_mehr: If you connect the output directly to IN−, the gain is exactly 1. This is called a voltage follower. It sounds boring, but it is useful: almost no current flows into the input, but the output can deliver a lot. That way you don't disturb a source.
exp2_5_5_w1: Take both resistors out and connect the output directly to IN−. How big is K2 now?
exp2_5_5_w2: Replace the 10 kΩ resistor with a 47 kΩ one. Work out beforehand what should come out.
exp2_5_5_echt: A microphone preamplifier often works like this. The tone stays the right way round, and the microphone is hardly loaded.
exp2_5_6_frage: Two signals lead through resistors to the same input IN−: a high tone from the generator and a low hum from the AC source. What comes out at the output?
exp2_5_6_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_5_6_b1: At the output both signals were mixed.
exp2_5_6_b2: At the output there was only one signal.
exp2_5_6_s1: Power the op-amp module with plus and minus as in the last experiment. Connect IN+ (M3) to 0V.
exp2_5_6_s2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and A3 and the 100 kΩ one into B1 and B3. Connect A3 to B3 and A3 to IN− (M4). Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A4 and A5. Connect A3 to A4 and the output (M5) to A5.
exp2_5_6_s3: Connect G to A1 and W~a to B1 and W~b to 0V. Set the generator to sine with 1000 Hz and 0.5 V peak. Plug K1 onto A1 and K2 onto A5 and switch on the main switch.
exp2_5_6_h1: The AC source is set to 6 V~. The 100 kΩ resistor makes it ten times quieter than the generator.
exp2_5_6_h2: The oscilloscope is set to 5 ms per division. That way you see the slow hum and the fast tone at the same time.
exp2_5_6_loesung: K2 shows a slow wave at 50 Hz with the fast 1000 Hz tone riding on it. Together that is about 2.7 V peak-to-peak.
exp2_5_6_erklaerung: IN− stays almost exactly at 0 V. That is why the two inputs don't disturb each other. Each current flows on through the 10 kΩ resistor at the output, and there they add up. The generator comes through with 10 kΩ : 10 kΩ = 1 times, the hum with 10 kΩ : 100 kΩ = 0.1 times.
exp2_5_6_mehr: With one resistor per input you can mix as many signals as you like. Each input gets its own volume. This circuit is called a summing amplifier.
exp2_5_6_w1: Replace the 100 kΩ resistor with a 10 kΩ one. What does K2 look like now?
exp2_5_6_w2: Take out the wire to the AC source. What is left at the output?
exp2_5_6_echt: A mixing desk in a recording studio or at a concert mixes many microphones and instruments. There is a fader for each channel, just like the resistors here.
exp2_5_7_frage: Instead of the resistor from the output to IN−, there is now a capacitor. A square wave is at the input. What does the output look like?
exp2_5_7_v1: Like a triangle: straight ramps up and down.
exp2_5_7_v2: A square wave again, just bigger.
exp2_5_7_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_5_7_b1: There was a triangle at the output.
exp2_5_7_b2: There was a square wave at the output.
exp2_5_7_b3: The output stuck at the top or the bottom.
exp2_5_7_s1: Power the op-amp module with plus and minus as in the last experiment. Connect IN+ (M3) to 0V.
exp2_5_7_s2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and A2. Plug the 10 nF capacitor into A3 and A4 and the 1 MΩ resistor into B3 and B4. Connect A2 to A3 and A3 to B3 and A4 to B4.
exp2_5_7_s3: Connect A2 to IN− (M4) and the output (M5) to A4. Connect G to A1. Set square with 1000 Hz and 1 V peak. Plug K1 onto A1 and K2 onto A4 and switch on.
exp2_5_7_h1: The 1 MΩ resistor next to the capacitor stops the output from slowly drifting away.
exp2_5_7_h2: Look at K2: is the line between the peaks straight or curved?
exp2_5_7_loesung: K2 shows a triangle with about 5 V peak-to-peak. While the square wave is up, the output falls steadily. While it is down, the output rises steadily.
exp2_5_7_erklaerung: A fixed current flows through the 10 kΩ resistor, because IN− stays at 0 V. This current charges the capacitor steadily. That is why the voltage across the capacitor rises like a straight ramp. This is called an integrator. It adds up the current, so to speak.
exp2_5_7_mehr: An op-amp cannot change its output arbitrarily fast. This one manages about 0.5 V in one microsecond. This is called the slew rate. That is why at very high frequencies even square waves at the output become slanted.
exp2_5_7_w1: Set the generator to 500 Hz. Does the triangle get bigger or smaller?
exp2_5_7_w2: Set the generator to sine. What does the output look like now?
exp2_5_7_echt: Synthesizers make sounds from square, triangle and sine waves. There an integrator turns one into another.
exp2_5_8_frage: The tone is split: a low-pass filter lets the bass through, a high-pass filter the treble. P1 and P2 control them. The op-amp module mixes them again. Can you change the sound at the loudspeaker?
exp2_5_8_v1: Yes, the bass with P1 and the treble with P2.
exp2_5_8_v2: No, the loudspeaker always sounds the same.
exp2_5_8_v3: I don't know – I'll build it.
exp2_5_8_b1: P1 and P2 changed the sound and the curve.
exp2_5_8_s1: Power the op-amp module with plus and minus as in the last experiment. Connect IN+ (M3) to 0V. Low-pass: plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and A2 and the 100 nF capacitor into A3 and B3. Connect A2 to A3 and B3 to 0V.
exp2_5_8_s2: High-pass: plug the 10 nF capacitor into C1 and C2 and the 10 kΩ resistor into C3 and D3. Connect C2 to C3 and D3 to 0V. Connect A3 to P1b and C3 to P2b. Connect P1a to 0V and P2a to 0V.
exp2_5_8_s3: Connect P1s to A5 and P2s to C5. Plug 10 kΩ resistors into A5 and A6 and into C5 and C6. Connect A6 to B7 and C6 to B7 and B7 to IN− (M4). Plug the 47 kΩ resistor into B7 and B8. Connect the output (M5) to B8 and B8 to C9. Plug the 100 Ω resistor into C9 and D9. Connect D9 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Connect G to A1 and A1 to C1. Set square with 200 Hz and 1 V peak and switch on.
exp2_5_8_h1: A square wave contains many tones: the fundamental and many high overtones. That is why you can clearly hear what the controls do.
exp2_5_8_h2: Is your sound off? Look at K2: with P2 the edges get sharper, with P1 the flat parts get wider.
exp2_5_8_loesung: The loudspeaker shows 200 Hz. With P1 in the middle about 6.3 mA flow, with P1 fully up about 12 mA. If you turn up P2, sharp spikes appear at the edges: that is the treble.
exp2_5_8_erklaerung: The low-pass filter made of 10 kΩ and 100 nF only lets low tones through, below about 160 Hz. The high-pass filter made of 10 nF and 10 kΩ only lets high tones through, above about 1600 Hz. P1 and P2 take as much from each as you like. The op-amp module adds both together and amplifies them about 4.7 times.
exp2_5_8_mehr: You calculate the cut-off frequency with f = 1 : (2 · π · R · C). Try it in the formula calculator. Real tone controls are built a bit more cleverly, so that the sound stays completely unchanged in the middle position.
exp2_5_8_w1: Turn P1 fully up and P2 fully down. How does the tone sound? And the other way round?
exp2_5_8_w2: Replace the 100 nF capacitor with a 1 µF one. Does the bass get even deeper?
exp2_5_8_echt: A radio or a hi-fi system often has controls for bass and treble. Behind them are low-pass filters, high-pass filters and an amplifier, just like here.
exp2_6_1_frage: The 555 timer gets two resistors and an electrolytic capacitor. An LED hangs on the output. What does the LED do?
exp2_6_1_v2: It simply stays on all the time.
exp2_6_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_1_b1: The LED blinked by itself, about one and a half times a second.
exp2_6_1_b2: The LED stayed on all the time.
exp2_6_1_s1: Power the timer: connect V+ to + (M8) and to R (M4). Connect − (M1) to 0V.
exp2_6_1_s2: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and B1 and the 4.7 kΩ one into B1 and C1. Plug the electrolytic capacitor with plus on C1 and minus on D1. Connect V+ to A1 and D1 to 0V. Connect B1 to DIS (M7). Connect C1 to THR (M6) and C1 to TR (M2).
exp2_6_1_s3: Connect the output (M3) to A5. Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A5 and A6 and the red LED from A6 to A7 (long leg on A6). Connect A7 to 0V and switch on.
exp2_6_1_h1: The electrolytic capacitor charges through both resistors and discharges through the 4.7 kΩ resistor into DIS.
exp2_6_1_h2: Work out the blinking frequency in the formula calculator: f ≈ 1.44 : ((R1 + 2 · R2) · C).
exp2_6_1_loesung: The LED blinks about 1.5 times a second. The formula gives 1.44 : ((1 kΩ + 9.4 kΩ) · 100 µF) ≈ 1.4 Hz.
exp2_6_1_erklaerung: The capacitor slowly charges up. At two thirds of the supply, the 555 switches the output off and opens DIS. Now the capacitor discharges. At one third, the 555 switches on again. This goes on and on. Such a circuit is called astable, because it never comes to rest.
exp2_6_1_mehr: The 555 came on the market in 1972 and is still one of the most-built chips in the world. With larger resistors or a larger capacitor it blinks more slowly.
exp2_6_1_w1: Use 10 kΩ instead of 4.7 kΩ. Work out beforehand how fast it should blink then.
exp2_6_1_w2: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Does the blinking frequency change?
exp2_6_1_echt: Blinkers on bike trailers and road works often blink with exactly this kind of circuit.
exp2_6_2_frage: With the 555, are the light and the pause equally long? And can you change that with a diode?
exp2_6_2_v1: They are equally long, all by themselves.
exp2_6_2_v2: The light is longer. With the diode both become equally long.
exp2_6_2_v3: I don't know – I'll measure it.
exp2_6_2_b1: Without the diode the light was longer, with the diode both were almost equal.
exp2_6_2_b2: Light and pause were always equally long.
exp2_6_2_b3: With the diode the blinking stopped.
exp2_6_2_s1: Build the blinker as in the last experiment, but with two 4.7 kΩ resistors on A1 and B1 and on B1 and C1.
exp2_6_2_s2: Plug the diode from B2 to C2 (ring towards C2). Connect B1 to B2 and C1 to C2.
exp2_6_2_s3: Plug K1 onto A5 and switch on. Compare on the oscilloscope how long the output is up and how long it is down. Then take the diode out and compare again.
exp2_6_2_h1: Without the diode the capacitor charges through both resistors, but discharges through only one.
exp2_6_2_h2: With the diode, the charging current flows past the second resistor.
exp2_6_2_loesung: Without the diode the output is up about two thirds of the time. With the diode it is up almost exactly half of the time. The average at A5 drops from almost 5 V to about 3.9 V.
exp2_6_2_erklaerung: Charging goes through R1 and R2, discharging only through R2. That is why charging takes longer. The diode lets the charging current flow past R2. Now the capacitor charges only through R1 and discharges through R2. If both are the same size, pulse and pause are almost equally long.
exp2_6_2_mehr: The ratio of the pulse length to the whole period is called the duty cycle. 50 percent means: pulse and pause are equally long. The diode needs about 0.7 V, so it doesn't come out quite exactly equal.
exp2_6_2_w1: Use a 1 kΩ resistor on A1 and B1. How long is the pulse now compared with the pause?
exp2_6_2_w2: Turn the diode round. What happens?
exp2_6_2_echt: A car indicator is usually on just as long as it is off. That looks calm and is easy to see.
exp2_6_3_frage: The 555 compares the voltage across the capacitor. Between which voltages does it swing?
exp2_6_3_v1: Between one third and two thirds of the battery.
exp2_6_3_v3: I don't know – I'll have a look.
exp2_6_3_b1: The voltage swung between about 3 V and 6 V.
exp2_6_3_b2: The voltage swung between 0 V and 9 V.
exp2_6_3_b3: The voltage always stayed the same.
exp2_6_3_s1: Build the blinker as in »The 555 blinks«.
exp2_6_3_s2: Plug K1 onto C1 and K2 onto A5. Switch on.
exp2_6_3_s3: Tap the magnifier 🔍 on the timer (»Look inside«). Compare the voltages inside with the curve on K1.
exp2_6_3_h1: C1 is the capacitor, A5 is the output.
exp2_6_3_h2: Looking inside, you see three equal resistors, two comparators and a memory.
exp2_6_3_loesung: K1 shows a zigzag curve from about 3 V to 6 V. Every time it reaches the top, K2 jumps down. When it reaches the bottom, K2 jumps up.
exp2_6_3_erklaerung: Three equal resistors inside the 555 divide the 9 V into three parts: 3 V and 6 V. One comparator checks whether the capacitor goes above 6 V. The other checks whether it falls below 3 V. A small memory, the flip-flop, remembers which one triggered last. The output follows it.
exp2_6_3_mehr: You know the comparators from level 5: they work like the op-amp module as a comparator. Because the thresholds are always one third and two thirds of the supply, the 555 blinks almost as fast at 6 V as at 9 V.
exp2_6_3_w1: Set the battery to 4.5 V. Between which voltages does the capacitor swing now?
exp2_6_3_w2: Connect CV (M5) to 0V through a 10 kΩ resistor. What changes on K1?
exp2_6_3_echt: Inside the 555 there are about 25 transistors on a tiny chip. Here you only see what they do together.
exp2_6_4_frage: You tap a push button briefly. How long does the LED stay on?
exp2_6_4_v1: Only as long as I press.
exp2_6_4_v2: A fixed time, even after I have let go.
exp2_6_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_4_b1: The LED stayed on for a few seconds after I let go.
exp2_6_4_b2: The LED went off as soon as I let go.
exp2_6_4_b3: The LED didn't come on at all.
exp2_6_4_s1: Power the timer: connect V+ to + (M8) and to R (M4). Connect − (M1) to 0V.
exp2_6_4_s2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and B1 and the push button into B1 and C1. Connect V+ to A1 and C1 to 0V and B1 to TR (M2). Plug the 47 kΩ resistor into A3 and B3 and the electrolytic capacitor with plus on C3 and minus on D3. Connect V+ to A3 and B3 to C3 and D3 to 0V.
exp2_6_4_s3: Connect B3 to THR (M6) and B3 to DIS (M7). Build the LED at the output (M3) as in the first experiment. Switch on and tap the push button briefly.
exp2_6_4_h1: The 10 kΩ resistor holds TR up. The push button pulls TR down briefly. That starts the time.
exp2_6_4_h2: Count how long the LED stays lit.
exp2_6_4_loesung: After a short tap the LED stays lit for about 5 seconds. The formula gives t ≈ 1.1 · 47 kΩ · 100 µF ≈ 5.2 s.
exp2_6_4_erklaerung: The tap on TR sets the memory in the 555: the output comes on, DIS lets go. Now the capacitor charges through 47 kΩ. At two thirds of the supply, THR resets the memory. The output goes off, DIS discharges the capacitor. The circuit waits for the next tap. This is called monostable.
exp2_6_4_mehr: In Volta 1 you built a stairwell light with the timer module. Here the same thing is inside one chip. If you hold the push button down for a long time, the LED stays on as long as you press.
exp2_6_4_w1: Use a 100 kΩ resistor instead of 47 kΩ. Work out beforehand how long the LED should stay lit now.
exp2_6_4_w2: Hold the push button down for longer than 5 seconds. What happens?
exp2_6_4_echt: The light in a stairwell comes on for a while after you press the button and then goes off by itself. Many such timer switches work like this.
exp2_6_5_frage: A second LED hangs between plus and the output. A push button pulls R down. What happens?
exp2_6_5_v1: The LEDs blink alternately, the push button stops everything.
exp2_6_5_v2: Both LEDs blink at the same time.
exp2_6_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_5_b1: The LEDs blinked alternately. With the push button only the green one stayed on.
exp2_6_5_b2: Both LEDs blinked at the same time.
exp2_6_5_s1: Build the blinker as in »The 555 blinks«, but do not connect R (M4) to V+ yet.
exp2_6_5_s2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A3 and B3 and the push button into B3 and C3. Connect V+ to A3 and B3 to R (M4) and C3 to 0V.
exp2_6_5_s3: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into C7 and C6 and the green LED from C6 to C5 (long leg on C6). Connect V+ to C7 and C5 to A5. Switch on and then press the push button.
exp2_6_5_h1: When the output is up, the red LED lights. When it is down, current flows from plus through the green LED into the output.
exp2_6_5_h2: R means reset. If R is down, the output is always off, no matter what else happens.
exp2_6_5_loesung: Red and green blink alternately, about 1.5 times a second. If you press the push button, the output stays down: green stays lit, red is off.
exp2_6_5_erklaerung: The output of the 555 can deliver current and take in current. When up, it sends current through the red LED to 0V. When down, it pulls current from plus through the green LED towards itself. The reset has priority over everything else and holds the output down.
exp2_6_5_mehr: An output that can work in both directions is called a push-pull output. You know the idea from the output stage in level 4.
exp2_6_5_w1: Hold the push button down and then let go. Which LED does the blinking start with?
exp2_6_5_w2: Take the red LED out. Does the green one keep blinking anyway?
exp2_6_5_echt: A level crossing has two red lamps that blink alternately. That catches the eye better than a single flashing light.
exp2_6_6_titel: A memory with two push buttons
exp2_6_6_frage: No capacitor: one push button pulls TR down, another pulls R down. Does the 555 remember which push button was pressed last?
exp2_6_6_v1: Yes, the LED stays on or off until the other push button comes.
exp2_6_6_v2: No, the LED only lights while I press.
exp2_6_6_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_6_b1: The LED stayed on until I pressed the other push button.
exp2_6_6_b2: The LED only lit while I was pressing.
exp2_6_6_s1: Power the timer: connect V+ to + (M8) and − (M1) to 0V. Connect THR (M6) to 0V.
exp2_6_6_s2: Plug the 10 kΩ resistor into A1 and B1 and push button S1 into B1 and C1. Connect V+ to A1 and B1 to TR (M2) and C1 to 0V. Plug the second 10 kΩ resistor into A3 and B3 and push button S2 into B3 and C3. Connect V+ to A3 and B3 to R (M4) and C3 to 0V.
exp2_6_6_s3: Build the LED at the output (M3) as in the first experiment. Switch on and open the magnifier 🔍 on the timer. Tap S1 and then S2.
exp2_6_6_h1: S1 sets the memory, S2 clears it.
exp2_6_6_h2: Looking inside, you see the flip-flop flip over.
exp2_6_6_loesung: After a tap on S1 the LED lights and stays on. Only a tap on S2 switches it off. It then stays off until you press S1 again.
exp2_6_6_erklaerung: Inside the 555 there is a flip-flop. It knows two states and stays in the last one until it is switched. TR sets it to »on«, R sets it to »off«. Because the circuit stays still in both states, it is called bistable.
exp2_6_6_mehr: A flip-flop stores one bit, a one or a zero. A computer contains billions of them. You will learn more about this in the Zuse series.
exp2_6_6_w1: Press both push buttons at the same time. Which one wins?
exp2_6_6_w2: Switch the battery off and on again. Does the 555 still know what it had stored?
exp2_6_6_echt: Many devices have an on button and an off button. Behind them there is often a memory like this.
exp2_6_7_frage: With a much smaller capacitor the 555 blinks so fast that you can hear it. Can you change the pitch with P1?
exp2_6_7_v1: Yes, P1 makes the tone higher and lower.
exp2_6_7_v2: No, the pitch always stays the same.
exp2_6_7_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_7_b1: With P1 the tone got higher and lower.
exp2_6_7_s1: Power the timer: connect V+ to + (M8) and to R (M4). Connect − (M1) to 0V.
exp2_6_7_s2: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and B1 and the 4.7 kΩ one into B2 and C2. Plug the 100 nF capacitor into C3 and D3. Connect V+ to A1 and B1 to DIS (M7). Connect B1 to P1a and P1s to B2. Connect C2 to C3 and D3 to 0V. Connect C2 to THR (M6) and C2 to TR (M2).
exp2_6_7_s3: Connect the output (M3) to A5. Plug the 220 Ω resistor into A5 and A6. Connect A6 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Switch on and turn P1.
exp2_6_7_h1: Here P1 works as a variable resistor: the further you turn, the bigger it gets.
exp2_6_7_h2: Is your sound off? The loudspeaker still shows the pitch.
exp2_6_7_loesung: With P1 at 0.2 the loudspeaker shows about 980 Hz. All the way back it is about 1350 Hz, all the way up about 470 Hz.
exp2_6_7_erklaerung: The 100 nF capacitor is a thousand times smaller than the electrolytic capacitor. That is why it charges and discharges a thousand times faster. A blink turns into a tone. P1 makes the resistance bigger, then each charge and discharge takes longer and the tone gets lower.
exp2_6_7_mehr: A square-wave tone sounds buzzy because it has many overtones. You know that from the tone control in level 5.
exp2_6_7_w1: Use a 220 nF capacitor. Does the tone get higher or lower?
exp2_6_7_w2: Replace P1 with a light-dependent resistor. What does the tone do when you shine light on it?
exp2_6_7_echt: Old toys, door bells and alarm clock beepers often make their tones with a 555.
exp2_6_8_frage: Here the 555 blinks 100 times a second. P1 shifts how long the pulse and how long the pause is. What do you see at the LED?
exp2_6_8_v1: It gets brighter and dimmer without flickering.
exp2_6_8_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_8_b1: The LED got brighter and dimmer with P1.
exp2_6_8_b2: The LED blinked faster and slower.
exp2_6_8_s1: Power the timer: connect V+ to + (M8) and to R (M4). Connect − (M1) to 0V.
exp2_6_8_s2: Plug the 1 kΩ resistor into A1 and B1. Connect V+ to A1 and B1 to DIS (M7) and B1 to P1s. Plug one diode from A2 to B2 (ring towards B2) and one from B2 to B3 (ring towards B3). Connect P1a to A2 and B3 to P1b.
exp2_6_8_s3: Plug the 1 µF capacitor into B2 and C2. Connect C2 to 0V and B2 to THR (M6) and B2 to TR (M2). Build the LED at the output (M3) as in the first experiment. Plug K1 onto B2 and K2 onto A5. Switch on and turn P1.
exp2_6_8_h1: One diode only lets the charging current through, the other only the discharging current. P1 divides its resistance between the two.
exp2_6_8_h2: Look at K2: does the pulse get wider while the pause gets narrower?
exp2_6_8_loesung: The output switches about 100 times a second. With P1 at 0.1 it is up about 20 percent of the time, at 0.5 about half, at 0.9 almost 90 percent. The LED gets brighter accordingly.
exp2_6_8_erklaerung: Charging goes through one part of P1, discharging through the other. When you turn P1, one part gets bigger and the other smaller. The pulse gets longer, the pause shorter, the whole period stays almost the same. Your eye is too slow for 100 flashes a second and only sees the average brightness.
exp2_6_8_mehr: This method is called pulse-width modulation, PWM for short. It is used to dim LEDs and control motors without wasting a lot of heat in a resistor: the output is always fully on or fully off.
exp2_6_8_w1: Use a 100 nF capacitor. Do you see a difference on the oscilloscope now? At the LED?
exp2_6_8_w2: Switch on slow motion. Now you can see the LED blinking.
exp2_6_8_echt: Many LED lamps and screens are dimmed with PWM. In a phone video you can sometimes see it as stripes.
exp2_6_9_frage: The red LED flashes only very briefly. The green LED only comes on if you press exactly during the flash. Can you do it?
exp2_6_9_v1: Yes, with a bit of practice I hit the flash.
exp2_6_9_v2: No, the flash is far too short.
exp2_6_9_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_6_9_b1: I sometimes hit the flash, then green lit up too.
exp2_6_9_b3: The red LED didn't flash at all.
exp2_6_9_s1: Build the blinker as in »Pulse and pause« with the diode, but with 1 kΩ on A1 and B1 and 22 kΩ on B1 and C1.
exp2_6_9_s2: Build the red LED at the output (M3) as in the first experiment.
exp2_6_9_s3: Plug the push button into B5 and B6 and connect A5 to B5. Plug the green LED from B6 to B7 (long leg on B6) and the 1 kΩ resistor into B7 and B8. Connect B8 to 0V. Switch on and try to press during the flash.
exp2_6_9_h1: The pulse is short because the capacitor charges through 1 kΩ and the diode. The pause is long because it discharges through 22 kΩ.
exp2_6_9_h2: The green LED only gets current when the output is up and you press at the same time.
exp2_6_9_loesung: About every 1.7 seconds red flashes for about 0.08 seconds. Only someone who presses at exactly that moment sees green light up.
exp2_6_9_erklaerung: Pulse and pause depend on two different resistors. With the diode the capacitor charges only through 1 kΩ, so quickly, and discharges through 22 kΩ, so slowly. The push button and the green LED hang on the output: there is only current when both come together.
exp2_6_9_mehr: People need about 0.2 seconds to react to a light signal. With a flash of 0.08 seconds you have to guess ahead when it is coming.
exp2_6_9_w1: Make the flash longer: use 2.2 kΩ instead of 1 kΩ on A1 and B1. Does it get easier?
exp2_6_9_w2: Let someone else press. Who hits it more often?
exp2_6_9_echt: At sports starts and in games, reaction time is often measured. Good sprinters start about 0.15 seconds after the shot.
exp2_7_1_frage: The blink module from Volta 1 contains two transistors and two electrolytic capacitors. Can you build it yourself?
exp2_7_1_v1: Yes, then the two LEDs blink alternately.
exp2_7_1_v2: No, without the module nothing blinks.
exp2_7_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_1_b1: The red and the green LED blinked alternately.
exp2_7_1_b2: Both LEDs stayed on all the time.
exp2_7_1_s1: Plug transistor T1 onto D3 and transistor T2 onto D7. Connect E4 and E8 to 0V.
exp2_7_1_s2: Plug 1 kΩ into A4 and B4 and the red LED from B4 to D4 (long leg on B4). Plug 1 kΩ into A8 and B8 and the green LED from B8 to D8 (long leg on B8). Plug 4.7 kΩ into B3 and D3 and 5.6 kΩ into B7 and D7. Connect V+ to A4, A8, B3 and B7.
exp2_7_1_s3: Plug one electrolytic capacitor with plus on D5 and minus on D6, the second with plus on C6 and minus on C5. Connect D4 to D5, D6 to D7, D8 to C6 and C5 to D3. Switch on.
exp2_7_1_h1: Each capacitor leads from the collector of one transistor to the base of the other. That way the two switch each other.
exp2_7_1_h2: Switch on slow motion and put K1 on D3. Then you can see the base flip.
exp2_7_1_loesung: The LEDs blink alternately, about 1.6 times a second. The rule of thumb f ≈ 1 : (0.69 · (R1 + R2) · C) gives about 1.4 Hz. The LEDs make the voltage jump a little smaller, so it blinks a bit faster.
exp2_7_1_erklaerung: When T1 conducts, its collector jumps to almost 0 V. The capacitor passes this jump on to the base of T2: it falls far below 0 V, and T2 turns off. Through 5.6 kΩ the capacitor recharges until the base reaches 0.7 V again. Then T2 conducts, and the same thing happens the other way round. The two resistors are different on purpose, so that the circuit is sure to start.
exp2_7_1_mehr: This circuit is called an astable multivibrator. It is more than a hundred years old and was first built with valves. The blink module contains the same circuit, just with smaller capacitors.
exp2_7_1_w1: Replace 4.7 kΩ with 10 kΩ. Which LED stays on longer now?
exp2_7_1_w2: Make both resistors the same: 4.7 kΩ. Does the circuit still start?
exp2_7_1_echt: Warning lights at road works and old bike indicators often worked with exactly this two-transistor circuit.
exp2_7_2_frage: The same multivibrator gets capacitors that are a thousand times smaller. What do you hear?
exp2_7_2_v1: A tone, because it now flips much faster.
exp2_7_2_v2: Nothing, because the capacitors are too small.
exp2_7_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_2_s1: Plug transistor T1 onto D3 and transistor T2 onto D7. Connect E4 and E8 to 0V. Plug 1 kΩ into A4 and B4 and the red LED from B4 to D4 (long leg on B4). Connect V+ to A4.
exp2_7_2_s2: Plug 10 kΩ into B3 and D3 and 12 kΩ into B7 and D7. Connect V+ to B3 and B7. Plug the 100 nF capacitor into D5 and D6 and the second one into C5 and C6. Connect D4 to D5, D6 to D7, D8 to C6 and C5 to D3.
exp2_7_2_s3: Connect V+ to LS1 and LS2 to A8. Plug 470 Ω into A8 and B8 and connect B8 to D8. Switch on.
exp2_7_2_h1: The multivibrator is the same as before, only the capacitors are smaller. At T2 the loudspeaker sits in place of the LED.
exp2_7_2_h2: Is your sound off? The loudspeaker still shows the pitch.
exp2_7_2_loesung: The loudspeaker shows about 680 Hz. The rule of thumb gives 1 : (0.69 · 22 kΩ · 100 nF) ≈ 660 Hz. The red LED flips just as fast and so seems simply to be on.
exp2_7_2_erklaerung: 100 nF is a thousand times less than 100 µF. That is why each capacitor recharges a thousand times faster. A blink turns into a tone of several hundred vibrations a second. The tone module from Volta 1 plays its tones on the same principle, with a little melody added.
exp2_7_2_mehr: Volta works out the tone from the simulated circuit and plays exactly that frequency. The tone sounds buzzy: it is almost a square wave and has many overtones.
exp2_7_2_w1: Replace both capacitors with 220 nF. Does the tone get higher or lower?
exp2_7_2_w2: Replace 12 kΩ with 22 kΩ. What changes in the tone?
exp2_7_2_echt: Simple buzzers in alarm clocks, toys and smoke alarms often contain such a multivibrator.
exp2_7_3_frage: A slow 555 switches a fast 555 via CV. What do you hear?
exp2_7_3_v1: Two tones taking turns, like a siren.
exp2_7_3_v2: One tone that always stays the same.
exp2_7_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_3_b1: It sounded high and low by turns.
exp2_7_3_b2: The tone always stayed the same.
exp2_7_3_s1: Power both timers: connect V+ to + and R of TI1 (M8, M4) and of TI2 (M16, M12). Connect − of TI1 (M1) and of TI2 (M9) to 0V.
exp2_7_3_s2: Build the blinker with TI1 as in »The 555 blinks«: 1 kΩ on A1 and B1, 4.7 kΩ on B1 and C1, electrolytic capacitor with plus on C1 and minus on D1. Build the same with TI2 in column 3, but with the 100 nF capacitor on C3 and D3. In each case connect V+ to A, B to DIS, C to THR and TR and D to 0V.
exp2_7_3_s3: Connect the output of TI2 (M11) to A5. Plug 220 Ω into A5 and A6, connect A6 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Connect the output of TI1 (M3) to A8, plug 10 kΩ into A8 and A9 and connect A9 to CV of TI2 (M13). Switch on.
exp2_7_3_h1: CV is the middle of the voltage divider inside the 555. If you pull CV higher, both thresholds are higher. Then each recharge takes longer.
exp2_7_3_h2: Measure with K1 on A9 or look at the pitch on the loudspeaker.
exp2_7_3_loesung: A9 jumps back and forth between about 4.5 V and 6.3 V. At 4.5 V TI2 plays about 1.8 kHz, at 6.3 V about 1.3 kHz. It sounds like a siren, about 1.5 times a second.
exp2_7_3_erklaerung: TI1 blinks slowly. When its output is up, it pulls CV of TI2 up through 10 kΩ. When it is down, it pulls CV down. The thresholds of TI2 move with it: if they are higher, the capacitor needs longer and the tone gets lower. That way one timer switches the other between two tones.
exp2_7_3_mehr: Without CV the thresholds are at one and two thirds of the supply. With CV you can shift them without swapping a resistor. This is called frequency modulation.
exp2_7_3_w1: Replace 10 kΩ on A8 and A9 with 4.7 kΩ. Are the two tones further apart now?
exp2_7_3_w2: Replace the electrolytic capacitor of TI1 with the 1 µF capacitor. What do you hear now?
exp2_7_3_echt: The sirens of police cars and fire engines switch between two tones. Today a chip usually produces that.
exp2_7_4_frage: There is now an electrolytic capacitor between TI1 and CV of TI2. Does the pitch still jump, or does it glide?
exp2_7_4_v1: It glides slowly up and down.
exp2_7_4_v2: It jumps like the two-tone siren.
exp2_7_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_4_b1: The tone wailed slowly up and down.
exp2_7_4_b2: The tone jumped between two pitches.
exp2_7_4_s1: Build the two-tone siren, but with 22 kΩ instead of 4.7 kΩ on B1 and C1. Leave out the resistor on A8 and A9.
exp2_7_4_s2: Plug 22 kΩ into A8 and B8 and the electrolytic capacitor with plus on B8 and minus on C8. Connect the output of TI1 (M3) to A8 and C8 to 0V.
exp2_7_4_s3: Plug 4.7 kΩ into B9 and B10. Connect B8 to B9 and B10 to CV of TI2 (M13). Switch on and listen.
exp2_7_4_h1: The capacitor cannot jump. It charges and discharges slowly through 22 kΩ.
exp2_7_4_h2: Put K1 on B8. The curve rises and falls in arcs.
exp2_7_4_loesung: TI1 flips about every 1.5 seconds. The voltage on B8 rises and falls between about 4.5 V and 6.2 V. The tone glides along, roughly between 1.3 kHz and 1.8 kHz.
exp2_7_4_erklaerung: In the two-tone siren, CV jumped with the output of TI1. Now there is a capacitor in between. It charges slowly when TI1 is up and discharges slowly when TI1 is down. CV follows this curve, and the pitch glides with it. That makes a wailing tone.
exp2_7_4_mehr: The resistor and capacitor form an RC network, like the low-pass filter from level 2. It smooths the jumps into gentle arcs.
exp2_7_4_w1: Replace 22 kΩ on A8 and B8 with 47 kΩ. Does the tone wail further or less far now?
exp2_7_4_w2: Replace 22 kΩ on B1 and C1 with 47 kΩ. What changes?
exp2_7_4_echt: Sirens during test alarms and some burglar alarms wail up and down just like this.
exp2_7_5_frage: So far all the tones were almost square waves. Can the op-amp module produce a soft sine tone?
exp2_7_5_v2: No, circuits always make square waves.
exp2_7_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_5_b1: The oscilloscope showed a soft sine curve.
exp2_7_5_b2: The oscilloscope showed a square wave.
exp2_7_5_s1: Give the op-amp module plus and minus: connect V+ to + (M1) and − (M2) to −B2. Connect +B2 to 0V. Plug 10 kΩ into A1 and A2 and 10 nF into A2 and A3. Plug 10 kΩ into B3 and C3 and 10 nF into B4 and C4. Connect A3 to B3, B3 to B4, C3 to C4, C4 to 0V and B3 to IN+ (M3).
exp2_7_5_s2: Plug 10 kΩ into D1 and D2, 10 kΩ into D2 and D3 and 15 kΩ into D3 and D4. Connect D1 to 0V, D2 to IN− (M4) and the output (M5) to A1. Connect D4 to A1.
exp2_7_5_s3: Plug one diode from E3 to E4 (ring towards E4) and one from C5 to C6 (ring towards C6). Connect D3 to E3, E4 to D4, D4 to C5 and C6 to D3. Plug 220 Ω into C1 and C2, connect A1 to C1, C2 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Plug K1 onto A1 and switch on.
exp2_7_5_h1: The resistors and capacitors at IN+ are called a Wien bridge. They let only one frequency through properly, and a third of it at that.
exp2_7_5_h2: The op-amp amplifies about three times. The diodes slow it down when the oscillation gets too big.
exp2_7_5_loesung: K1 shows a sine wave of about 1.6 kHz and a good 1 V peak. The formula f = 1 : (2π · R · C) gives 1 : (2π · 10 kΩ · 10 nF) ≈ 1.6 kHz.
exp2_7_5_erklaerung: Part of the output goes back to IN+ through the Wien bridge. At exactly one frequency, a third arrives without any shift. The op-amp amplifies a little more than three times, so the oscillation grows by itself. When it gets big, the diodes conduct and the gain drops to exactly three. The oscillation then stays the same size and nicely round.
exp2_7_5_mehr: In real life the tiny noise of the components gives the first push. You can work out the frequency in the formula calculator under »Cut-off frequency«: the formula is the same as for the low-pass filter.
exp2_7_5_w1: Replace both 10 nF capacitors with 22 nF. How high is the tone now?
exp2_7_5_w2: Take out one diode. What happens to the curve?
exp2_7_5_echt: Tone generators in workshops and the dial tone of the telephone used to be sine circuits like this.
exp2_7_6_frage: With one 555, two push buttons and the knobs P1 and P2 you build an instrument. Can you play it?
exp2_7_6_v1: Yes, with the push buttons and knobs I change the tone and the volume.
exp2_7_6_v2: No, a 555 only ever makes one tone.
exp2_7_6_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_7_6_b1: S1 played, S2 made the tone lower, P1 and P2 changed pitch and volume.
exp2_7_6_b2: It always made the same tone.
exp2_7_6_s1: Build the tone generator as in »A tone from the chip«: 1 kΩ on A1 and B1, 4.7 kΩ on B2 and C2, 100 nF on C3 and D3. Connect V+ to A1, B1 to DIS (M7) and P1a, P1s to B2, C2 to C3, THR (M6) and TR (M2) and D3 to 0V. Connect V+ to + (M8) and − (M1) to 0V.
exp2_7_6_s2: Plug the second 100 nF into C4 and D4 and push button S2 into D4 and E4. Connect C3 to C4 and E4 to 0V. Plug 10 kΩ into A8 and B8 and push button S1 into B8 and C8. Connect A8 to 0V, B8 to R (M4) and V+ to C8.
exp2_7_6_s3: Connect the output (M3) to A5. Plug 220 Ω into A5 and A6 and the 1 µF capacitor into A6 and A7. Connect A7 to P2a, P2s to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Switch on, hold S1 and play with S2, P1 and P2.
exp2_7_6_h1: S1 is the play key: the 555 only oscillates while R is up. S2 adds a second capacitor.
exp2_7_6_h2: P1 changes the pitch, P2 is in series with the loudspeaker and is the volume. The 1 µF capacitor is a tone filter.
exp2_7_6_loesung: With S1 and P1 at 0.2 the loudspeaker plays about 980 Hz. With S2 as well it is about 490 Hz, an octave lower. P2 makes the tone quieter, P1 shifts it.
exp2_7_6_erklaerung: S1 lifts the reset: only then does the 555 oscillate. If you press S2, two capacitors are side by side. Recharging takes twice as long, and the tone drops an octave. P2 holds back the current to the loudspeaker. The 1 µF capacitor lets high tones through more easily than low ones. That is why low tones sound quieter and thinner.
exp2_7_6_mehr: A synthesizer shapes sounds out of electrical oscillations. The first synthesizers of the 1960s were made of oscillators, filters and amplifiers, just like your little instrument.
exp2_7_6_w1: Replace the 1 µF capacitor with a wire. How do the low tones sound now?
exp2_7_6_w2: Play a little tune using only S1, S2 and P1. Can you manage »Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star«?
exp2_7_6_echt: Electronic organs and keyboards make their tones with oscillators and filters. Today a chip usually calculates that.
exp2_8_1_frage: An IR LED and a red LED get the same current. Do both light up?
exp2_8_1_v2: The IR LED shines too, but you cannot see its light.
exp2_8_1_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_8_1_b1: Both LEDs got current, but only the red one lit up visibly.
exp2_8_1_b3: No current flowed through the IR LED.
exp2_8_1_s1: Plug 1 kΩ into A1 and A2, the current measuring point into A2 and A3 and the IR LED from A3 to A4 (long leg on A3). Connect V+ to A1 and A4 to 0V.
exp2_8_1_s2: Plug 1 kΩ into C1 and C2, the second current measuring point into C2 and C3 and the red LED from C3 to C4 (long leg on C3). Connect V+ to C1 and C4 to 0V.
exp2_8_1_s3: Switch on. Compare the two currents on the dual meter and look at the LEDs.
exp2_8_1_h1: The dashed rays on the IR LED show: it is shining, but your eye cannot see it.
exp2_8_1_h2: The IR LED needs only about 1.3 V, the red one about 1.9 V. That is why a little more current flows through the IR LED.
exp2_8_1_loesung: About 7.7 mA flow through the IR LED and about 7.2 mA through the red one. The red one shines visibly, the IR LED seemingly not at all.
exp2_8_1_erklaerung: Light is radiation with different colours. Red has the longest wavelength our eye can still see. The IR LED gives off infrared, which has an even longer wavelength. Our eye has no sensory cells for it. The radiation is still there and carries energy, just like visible light.
exp2_8_1_mehr: Infrared means »below red«. The warmth you feel in front of a stove is also infrared radiation, only with an even longer wavelength.
exp2_8_1_w1: Replace the 1 kΩ in front of the IR LED with 470 Ω. How much current flows now?
exp2_8_1_w2: Turn the IR LED round. Does current still flow?
exp2_8_1_echt: Point a phone camera at a remote control and press a button. Often the front camera shows the glow best.
exp2_8_2_frage: The IR LED shines on a phototransistor. What happens to its current when the IR LED gets weaker?
exp2_8_2_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_8_2_b1: The current through the phototransistor got smaller when the IR LED got weaker.
exp2_8_2_s1: Plug the IR LED from A4 to A2 (long leg on A4) and 470 Ω into A5 and A4. Connect V+ to P1a, P1s to A5 and A2 to 0V.
exp2_8_2_s2: Plug the phototransistor from B4 to B2 (C on B4, E on B2), right below the IR LED. Connect B2 to 0V.
exp2_8_2_s3: Plug 1 kΩ into B4 and C4 and the current measuring point into C4 and C5. Connect V+ to C5. Switch on and slowly turn P1 up.
exp2_8_2_h1: Here P1 is a variable resistor in front of the IR LED. The further you turn, the less current it gets.
exp2_8_2_h2: Room light and the torch also act on the phototransistor. Try it in the bar »Light, heat, water«.
exp2_8_2_loesung: With P1 at 0, about 16 mA flow through the IR LED and about 2 mA through the phototransistor. With P1 at 0.5 it is only about 0.3 mA.
exp2_8_2_erklaerung: A phototransistor has no base connection. Instead, light falls on its base. Each particle of light frees a few charges there. They act like a small base current, and the transistor amplifies it. The more radiation arrives, the more current it lets through from C to E.
exp2_8_2_mehr: A light-dependent resistor from Volta 1 reacts slowly, in tenths of a second. A phototransistor reacts in millionths of a second. That is why it can also receive fast signals, even music.
exp2_8_2_w1: Put the cover card between the IR LED and the phototransistor. What does the current measuring point show?
exp2_8_2_w2: Plug the phototransistor two rows lower. How much does the distance matter?
exp2_8_2_echt: Every television has an infrared receiver. It works like your phototransistor.
exp2_8_3_frage: The phototransistor holds the reset of the 555 down as long as IR light arrives. What happens when you interrupt the radiation?
exp2_8_3_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_8_3_b1: With the card in between a tone sounded, without the card it was silent.
exp2_8_3_b2: The tone played all the time.
exp2_8_3_s1: Plug the IR LED from A4 to A2 (long leg on A4) and 1 kΩ into A5 and A4. Connect V+ to A5 and A2 to 0V. Plug the phototransistor from B4 to B2 (C on B4) and connect B2 to 0V.
exp2_8_3_s2: Plug 22 kΩ into C4 and D4. Connect B4 to C4, V+ to D4 and B4 to R (M4). Power the timer: V+ to + (M8), − (M1) to 0V. Build the tone generator in column 6: 1 kΩ on A6 and B6, 4.7 kΩ on B6 and C6, 100 nF on C6 and D6. Connect V+ to A6, B6 to DIS (M7), C6 to THR (M6) and TR (M2), D6 to 0V.
exp2_8_3_s3: Connect the output (M3) to A8, plug 220 Ω into A8 and A9, connect A9 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. The cover card is already standing over the phototransistor. Switch on, slide the card away and back again.
exp2_8_3_h1: When IR light arrives, the phototransistor conducts and pulls R down. Then the 555 is silent.
exp2_8_3_h2: You will find the cover card in the bar »Light, heat, water«.
exp2_8_3_loesung: Without the card R is at about 0.1 V and the loudspeaker is silent. With the card R rises to almost 9 V, and the loudspeaker plays about 1.35 kHz.
exp2_8_3_erklaerung: The phototransistor and the 22 kΩ resistor form a voltage divider. When radiation arrives, the phototransistor conducts strongly and R is almost at 0 V. The card casts a shadow: the phototransistor turns off, the resistor pulls R up, and the 555 oscillates.
exp2_8_3_mehr: Light barriers almost always work with infrared. You can't see the beam, and room light disturbs it less. Often the IR LED also blinks fast so that the receiver can tell it apart from the sun.
exp2_8_3_w1: Replace 22 kΩ with 4.7 kΩ. Does the light barrier still work?
exp2_8_3_w2: Set the room light to »dark«. Does anything change?
exp2_8_3_echt: Lift doors, garage doors and shop doors have light barriers. They notice when someone is in the way.
exp2_8_4_frage: An optocoupler contains an IR LED and a phototransistor. Can a push button on battery 1 switch an LED on battery 2, with no wire in between?
exp2_8_4_v1: Yes, the light inside the optocoupler carries the signal.
exp2_8_4_v2: No, without a wire no signal gets across.
exp2_8_4_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_8_4_b1: With the push button pressed, the green LED on battery 2 lit up.
exp2_8_4_b3: The green LED lit up even without the push button.
exp2_8_4_s1: Plug the optocoupler onto B2. Plug the push button into A1 and A2 and 1 kΩ into A2 and B2. Connect V+ to A1 and C2 to 0V.
exp2_8_4_s2: Plug 1 kΩ into A5 and A4 and the green LED from A4 to A3 (long leg on A4). Connect +B2 to A5, A3 to B3 and C3 to −B2.
exp2_8_4_s3: Switch on and press the push button. Check: is there a wire between the two circuits?
exp2_8_4_h1: On the left of the optocoupler sits the IR LED (A and K), on the right the phototransistor (C and E).
exp2_8_4_h2: The circuit with the push button runs on battery 1, the circuit with the green LED on battery 2.
exp2_8_4_loesung: With the push button pressed, about 6.8 mA flow through the green LED. When you let go, it goes off. There is no wire between the two circuits.
exp2_8_4_erklaerung: The push button switches on the IR LED inside the optocoupler. Its light falls on the phototransistor in the dark housing, and the transistor conducts. That way light carries the signal from one circuit to the other. The two circuits share no wire: we say they are galvanically isolated.
exp2_8_4_mehr: In Volta 1 the relay did something similar, with a magnet instead of light. An optocoupler has no moving parts, is much faster and doesn't click.
exp2_8_4_w1: Replace the 1 kΩ on A2 and B2 with 10 kΩ. Is the green LED still as bright?
exp2_8_4_w2: Set battery 2 to 4.5 V. What changes at the green LED?
exp2_8_4_echt: In chargers and power supplies, optocouplers separate the dangerous mains voltage from the part you can touch.
exp2_8_5_frage: The generator controls the brightness of the IR LED. Does the tone arrive at the loudspeaker over the light path?
exp2_8_5_v1: Yes, the phototransistor picks up the flicker and turns it back into a tone.
exp2_8_5_v3: I don't know – I'll try it out.
exp2_8_5_b1: The loudspeaker played the tone of the generator.
exp2_8_5_s1: Set the generator to sine, 440 Hz, 1 V peak and 2.5 V DC offset. Plug the IR LED from A4 to A2 (long leg on A4) and 220 Ω into A5 and A4. Connect G to A5 and A2 to 0V.
exp2_8_5_s2: Plug the phototransistor from B4 to B2 (C on B4) and 4.7 kΩ into B4 and C4. Connect B2 to 0V and V+ to C4. Plug 1 µF into B5 and B6 and 100 kΩ into B6 and C6. Connect B4 to B5 and C6 to 0V.
exp2_8_5_s3: Power the op-amp module: V+ to + (M1), − (M2) to −B2, +B2 to 0V. Connect B6 to IN+ (M3) and the output (M5) to IN− (M4). Connect the output to A8, plug 100 Ω into A8 and A9, connect A9 to LS1 and LS2 to 0V. Plug K1 onto A5 and K2 onto B4 and switch on.
exp2_8_5_h1: The DC offset always keeps the IR LED a little on. The sine makes it brighter and dimmer in time.
exp2_8_5_h2: Here the op-amp module works as a voltage follower: the output does exactly what arrives at IN+, but it can deliver more current.
exp2_8_5_loesung: K2 shows a sine wave at the phototransistor of a good 3 V peak to peak and 440 Hz. The loudspeaker plays 440 Hz, the concert pitch A.
exp2_8_5_erklaerung: The generator makes the IR LED brighter and dimmer 440 times a second. The phototransistor follows the brightness exactly, and an AC voltage appears again across the 4.7 kΩ resistor. The capacitor lets only the AC voltage through. The op-amp module gives the loudspeaker the current it needs.
